fixes.explanation: David doesn't ask for a sign anywhere in this psalm. His very first request is “Have mercy on me, O God…” The heading names Nathan, the prophet who came to him, and David turns straight to God. He asks for mercy, and he asks it according to God's loving devotion.

David is a king (2 Samuel 5:3), so I can see why victory sounds like a good guess. But the psalm never mentions a battle. The first thing he says is “Have mercy on me, O God…” and then he asks God to blot out his transgressions.

The heading names Nathan, the prophet who came to David, but David doesn't name him in the prayer itself. Look at what David says to God: “Against You, You only, have I sinned…” He puts the word only right there. The one he names is God.

David is Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), so Israel is a natural guess. But the psalm never names the nation here. David says, “Against You, You only, have I sinned…” That word only points to one person, and it's God.
Enemies don't show up in this verse. David says, “Hide Your face from my sins…” This verse is about his own sin, not anyone chasing him. He keeps the focus where it belongs.
David is a king (2 Samuel 5:3), so the throne is a fair guess. But the verse says, “Cast me not away from Your presence…” He doesn't mention his crown or his throne. He's asking about God.

Return to God. David says, “Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You.” He wants to help other people find their way back. Someone asking God for mercy and then pointing others to that same God, that's the picture.
David says the opposite. He says, “Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You.” Instead of hiding, they come back. He says sinners will turn toward God.
Jericho is a city in the Bible (Joshua 6:1), but it isn't the one in this verse. David prays, “build up the walls of Jerusalem.” That's the city he names alongside Zion.
